title: Churchill and de Gaulle in Paris

facts.text: On 11 November 1944, Armistice Day, Winston Churchill and General Charles de Gaulle rode together up the Champs-Elysees in Paris, less than three months after the city was freed from German occupation.
Churchill had arrived the afternoon before at Orly with his wife Clementine and daughter Mary, and de Gaulle met them with a guard of honor.
At 10:45 a.m. the two leaders set out in open cars from the War Ministry, across the Seine, through the Place de la Concorde, and up the avenue.
Soldiers lined the route, and Parisians packed the sidewalks, windows, and rooftops, chanting 'Vive de Gaulle! Vive Churchill!' Churchill waved and gave his V sign.
Some members of Churchill's cabinet had tried to talk him out of going, since German stragglers were thought to be hiding in the city.
At the Arc de Triomphe, the two men laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and stood at the salute through a minute of silence.
They then walked through the crowd to watch an hour long parade of French, British, American, Canadian, Moroccan, and Algerian troops.
At a lunch afterward, Churchill, with tears in his eyes, said it gave him great pleasure 'to see Paris again, this Paris which is a brilliant star shining above the world.'
Just weeks earlier, on 23 October 1944, Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union had recognized de Gaulle's Provisional Government of the French Republic.

An Army Signal Corps cameraman filmed the day: the crowds at the Arc, the leaders' cars arriving with a motorcycle escort, the ceremony under a huge tricolor, and Churchill and de Gaulle walking through the crowd.

No 5 Army Film and Photographic Unit, IWM BU 1292, Crown copyright expired, public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). photo.caption: De Gaulle talks with Churchill at the saluting stand as the Armistice Day parade passes.

declassified.fact: Churchill and his party stayed at the Quai d'Orsay, which the Germans had used during the occupation. He joked that he had a gold bath, while Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden had to make do with a silver one.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Army Signal Corps film 'Armistice Parade, Paris, France', 11 Nov 44 (shot card: special coverage, slate 'SPX-F Paris Unit 2, 11-11-44, with sound'). The NARA digital copy's audio track is effectively silent (about -83 dB), so treat it as silent. The file is the stretch from 0:40 to 6:20 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times: 0:00 to 0:10 crowd and troops by the Arc; 0:10 to 0:20 the leaders' open cars drive up with a motorcycle escort, the best moving opener (cars clearest at about 0:15 to 0:25); 0:30 to 1:05 cars push through the cheering crowd with flags; 1:05 to 1:30 marching men and crowds; 1:50 to 2:50 the ceremony at the Arc, salutes, the tricolor hanging in the arch; 3:00 to 3:15 a plane overhead; 4:00 to 4:20 the Arc with the giant flag; 4:50 to 5:10 Churchill and de Gaulle walk through the crowd after the ceremony; 5:30 to 5:40 the parade forms near the Arc. The slate (about 0:30 to 0:40 of the reel) is before the file starts.

body:
Some of his cabinet tried to talk him out of it. German stragglers were thought to be hiding in the city. Churchill went anyway, and Paris came out to meet him.

11 November 1944. On Armistice Day, less than three months after Paris was freed, Winston Churchill and General Charles de Gaulle rode together in open cars up the Champs-Elysees.

Parisians packed the sidewalks, windows, and rooftops, chanting "Vive de Gaulle! Vive Churchill!" Churchill waved and gave his V sign.

At the Arc de Triomphe the two men laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and stood at the salute through a minute of silence. Then they walked through the crowd to watch an hour long parade of French, British, American, Canadian, Moroccan, and Algerian troops.

At lunch afterward, with tears in his eyes, Churchill said it gave him great pleasure "to see Paris again, this Paris which is a brilliant star shining above the world."
